items.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: you can find that progression from Corelli, Lully, through Beethoven in the Fifth Symphony Second Movement. Rachmaninoff, and into pop song writing.

ctx.x: The Original Dixieland Jazz Band. Yeah. Notwithstanding the fact that you had many artists earlier than that. My focus has been, in fact since we were last together, my focus has been on the history of finger style guitar and the instruments. And I put out of folio last year with Hal Leonard called “The Evolution of Finger Style Guitar.” And I started with transcriptions of lute music from 1507 from Petrucci’s first folio of lute tablature, and then followed that through Baroque guitar and Renaissance guitar,…

me was how much the concept of the chord progression, like we experience it in jazz you know, rhythm changes or whatever, has its historical antecedents in the sixteenth century you had the Romanesque, the passa mezzo maderno — that these progressions actually still get used even today. You know the Romanesque being the kind of the foundation of the “Greensleeves” progression. And then in the baroque era the vihuela or the vihuelo d’espania progression, which the closest — the pop song that was written on that is…
Can I ask you, you’ve played with so many people, you’ve been around the world. Are you still a citizen of England?
